answer.query_text: Ocean tides occur because the Moon’s gravity pulls unevenly on Earth: it is strongest on the side facing the Moon, weaker at Earth’s center, and weakest on the far side. This difference, called the tidal force, stretches the oceans into two broad bulges, one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side. The far-side bulge is not caused by the Moon directly pulling water outward; rather, the Earth and Moon orbit their common center of mass, creating inertia that makes water tend to move away from Earth’s center on that side. Earth’s rotation carries coastlines through these bulges, producing regularly changing high and low tides instead of allowing water to remain permanently piled up. In reality, the ocean does not form two perfect global humps. Continents, underwater ridges, varying depths, friction, and the shape of ocean basins redirect and slow the water, causing tides to behave like enormous waves that rotate around ocean basins. Local tides may therefore occur once or twice daily and can differ greatly in height and timing. The Sun also contributes tidal forces, strengthening or weakening the Moon’s effect depending on their alignment. Thus, tides result from a continuously changing balance among differential gravity, inertia, Earth’s rotation, and the constrained movement of water around the planet.
answer.reference_text: The moon’s gravity pulls Earth’s oceans into two opposing bulges: one facing the moon and another on the opposite side, where inertia dominates. As the planet rotates daily through both water mounds, coastlines experience two high and two low tides.

answer.query_text: Tides arise because the Moon’s gravity pulls on different parts of Earth with slightly different strength and direction, rather than pulling the whole planet and ocean uniformly toward it. The Moon attracts the near side of Earth more strongly than it attracts Earth’s center, producing a bulge of ocean water toward the Moon. It attracts the far side less strongly than it attracts Earth’s center, so there is also a relative bulge on the far side. Earth and Moon orbit their common center of mass, and the motion of that orbit helps create this far-side effect; it is not simply water being flung away in a separate force. The solid Earth is affected too, although less visibly, while the mobile ocean adjusts around it. As Earth rotates beneath these two broad tidal bulges, most coastal locations pass through two high tides and two low tides during a lunar day. Water does not remain collected on the Moon-facing side because Earth’s gravity holds the oceans to the planet, the Moon’s pull is only a small difference across Earth’s diameter, and the rotating Earth continually carries shorelines into and out of the bulges. Continents, seafloor shape, coastline geometry, and resonance in ocean basins modify the timing and height of local tides, while the Sun also strengthens or weakens them.
answer.reference_text: The Moon’s gravity raises a tidal bulge on the side of Earth facing it, while differences in gravitational pull produce another on the far side. As Earth rotates through both bulges, most coasts experience two high tides each lunar day.

answer.query_text: The attendance increased from 20 to 30 people, a gain of 10. Because the original number was 20, the percentage increase was 10 ÷ 20 = 50%. When attendance later fell from 30 back to 20, the loss was still 10 people, but this time the starting number was 30. Therefore, the percentage decrease was 10 ÷ 30, or about 33.3%. The percentages differ because they are calculated using different starting amounts, even though the numerical change is the same.
answer.reference_text: You have 30 cents if you have 3 dimes. Each dime is worth 10 cents, so you can find the total by adding 10 + 10 + 10 = 30. You can also multiply the number of dimes by the value of each one: 3 × 10 = 30 cents. In dollars, that amount is written as $0.30. Counting your dimes by tens gives you the same answer: 10, 20, 30 cents.

answer.query_text: Mara returned the borrowed ladder just before dusk, carrying it across the wet alley to Mr. Vale’s narrow blue house. He thanked her, then noticed the silver paint on her sleeve. She admitted she had used the ladder to finish a mural her sister had begun before leaving town. Curious, he followed Mara to the courtyard, where painted swallows swept across a brick wall toward a golden horizon. Mr. Vale stood silently for a moment, blinking behind his thick glasses. “Your sister painted one of those birds on my shop years ago,” he said. From his pocket, he produced a faded photograph proving it. Then he smiled and mentioned a neighborhood supper beneath the mural that evening. Mara hesitated, looked at the gathering lights, and accepted his invitation.
answer.reference_text: Mara found the bowling ball behind a thrift store, gleaming beneath a torn blue tarp. At league night, she tried it. Strike. Then another. By the tenth frame, the crowd chanted her name. For weeks, Mara became unbeatable, winning trophies and money, until she noticed the ball whispering whenever it hit the pins: “One more.” During the championship, her opponent, elderly Mr. Vale, stared at it in horror. “That’s mine,” he said. “It never misses—but each strike steals a year from the bowler.” Mara suddenly understood her new gray hairs and aching knees. In the final frame, she rolled the ball gently into the gutter. It cracked, releasing a flash of stolen time. Mara became young again, and Mr. Vale smiled. She lost the match, but saved them both.

answer.query_text: Mara returned the borrowed ladder just before dusk, carrying it across Mr. Vale’s garden while rain tapped softly on the rhubarb leaves. She had used it to rescue a kite from the old oak, but the kite was gone now, swept toward the river with its red tail snapping behind it. Mr. Vale met her at the gate, surprisingly cheerful. He said the ladder had once belonged to his wife, who climbed it every spring to hang lanterns for the neighborhood picnic. From his pocket, he produced a small brass lantern, polished but unlit. “We’re hanging them again Saturday,” he said. Mara looked toward the darkening oak and imagined warm lights beneath its branches, the lost kite perhaps resting somewhere nearby. Smiling, she accepted his invitation.

answer.query_text: A battery stores usable energy in the chemical arrangement of its materials, not as a supply of electricity. Its electrodes and electrolyte contain substances that can react to form a lower-energy arrangement. When a flashlight’s switch closes the circuit, these reactions drive electrons through the external wires while ions move within the battery, completing the circuit. The battery maintains a voltage, allowing energy to be transferred electrically to the light source. In an LED flashlight, some of that energy becomes visible light and the rest becomes heat. As the battery operates, its chemical composition changes and its ability to maintain voltage declines. A rechargeable battery can largely reverse these chemical changes when an external power source supplies energy.
answer.reference_text: An electric car uses electricity stored in a rechargeable battery pack to power one or more electric motors. When you press the accelerator, the battery sends energy through an inverter, which controls the motor’s speed and torque. The motor turns the wheels directly or through gears. Regenerative braking recovers some energy, while charging replenishes the battery.

loader.selection: Join EXP041 eligibility by unique job_key; require assessment=CONTROLLED_TRAINING_CANDIDATE, split=train and model in Luna/Terra. Exact expected population 120 rows, 60 original prompt groups, 60 rows per admitted model.
loader.text: record.text unchanged; require its SHA256 == text_sha256 == raw_final_sha256 and attempt_path_project/final.txt bytes equal UTF8(text).
loader.label: model_requested, explicitly requested_only provenance; no serving-snapshot verification.
loader.group: base_prompt/prompt_group from original shared bank; normalized base body identity across old/new versions. Do not use variant_id, protocol_version, job_key, model or route as independent split units.

sparse.selection: Use existing label-blind stable ID hash selection, then re-cluster/recenter selected validation texts; do not subset dense final predictions.

Known true training groups may center training; validation groups must be inferred from unlabelled validation text with unchanged algorithm.
